subject: TrueCap #13 — out-of-state investing: what to actually outsource
preheader: The 4 jobs you can't skip · The 3 you should · Why most OOS investors fail at #2 · 3 deals

marketSnapshot.headline: Rate-cut anticipation continues, market positioning ahead of Fed
marketSnapshot.body: Two weeks out from the Fed meeting and the market is positioned for a cut — 30Y mortgage at 6.47%, DSCR loans at 8.1%, even hard-money rates softening from 11.5% to 11.0% for top-tier borrowers. Anecdotally hearing from contacts at three different lenders that loan-application volume is up 30-40% MoM as investors rush to lock in before October. Worth pausing on the FOMO question — locking rate at 6.47% is good if you're closing in the next 30-45 days; bad if your deal is still 60-90 days out. Most lenders' 60-day rate locks add 25-50bp.

dealSpotter.body: $165k 3/2 at $1,525. Property is in a B-tier neighborhood with an established local PM (5+ years), recently rehabbed (2023), and inspected. Sellable to an out-of-state investor because all the hard work is done. The premium for turnkey: you're paying maybe $8-12k more than you would for a comparable distressed property, but you skip the rehab risk, contractor-finding, and 4-month vacancy that would otherwise eat that delta. Worth it for OOS investor #1 or #2.

dealSpotter.address: Memphis, TN — High Point Terrace duplex
dealSpotter.body: $185k 2-unit. The cap rate is real but the property is C-tier — older systems, tenants who'll need active management, neighborhood with block-by-block variation. For an in-state investor with a property manager, this works. For an out-of-state investor doing this their first or second deal, the gap between paper cap rate and real return is wide enough to be painful. Local relationships matter more here than they do for the Brookside deal above.

$148k 3-unit. Detroit-Shoreway is gentrifying but unevenly. The asking-side numbers look great. The reality I keep hearing from local investors: vacancy here runs 18-24% (not the 8% you'd assume), bad-debt is 4-7% of GR, and capex on these older multi-family buildings averages 18-22% rather than the 8-10% reserve you'd budget. The 10.6% paper cap drops to 6.4% real for an absentee owner. Only worth pursuing if you have boots-on-the-ground.

qa.question: I live in CA. The math doesn't work locally. How do I OOS-invest without losing my shirt?
qa.answer: Four jobs you cannot outsource: (1) Underwriting — you do the math, not a sales agent or 'turnkey provider.' Their incentives are wrong. (2) Picking the metro — research the state landlord laws, eviction timelines, and 5-year demographic trends. Don't take an agent's word for 'this is a hot market.' (3) Hiring the PM — interview at least 3 before signing. Ask for references AND specifically the addresses of properties they currently manage so you can drive-by (or have a friend drive-by) to verify condition. (4) Setting the operating budget — you decide what reserves are reasonable, not your PM (who'd often prefer lower reserves so they look better). Three jobs you SHOULD outsource: (1) Boots-on-the-ground tasks — showings, maintenance coordination, tenant placement. (2) Legal compliance — state-specific lease forms, security deposit handling, fair housing process. (3) Bookkeeping — your PM should produce Schedule-E-ready statements monthly. The #1 OOS-investor failure mode: outsourcing item 1 from the first list (underwriting). The turnkey provider's deal is rarely the math you'd accept if you'd run it yourself.
